content: Across the country, schools struggle to recruit and retain talented teachers. These challenges are often described as a staffing problem. But new Gallup research points to a deeper issue: Too many educators question whether they matter to the communities they serve. Mattering is the fundamental human need to feel valued and to have an opportunity to contribute to others. When people feel like they matter, they thrive. When they don’t, they struggle. The new study, the first nationwide survey to focus on educator mattering, reveals what that struggle looks like in the classroom: Among educators who lack a sense of mattering, 68% are frequently burned out, and fewer than half plan to remain in the profession long-term. Get stories like this delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up for The 74 Newsletter Over eight years of researching my book, Mattering: The Secret to a Life of Deep Connection and Purpose , I’ve spoken with hundreds of educators around the country who feel passionate about their work and students but unappreciated and underinvested-in as people. The findings of the Gallup poll, commissioned by the Walton Family Foundation, match what I’ve heard. Of 1,952 K-12 classroom teachers, teaching assistants, substitutes and paraprofessionals surveyed, only 35% said they matter a great deal at their school. Just 1 in 5 said someone at their school invests a great deal in their growth and development. Only 25% of respondents said they received appreciation from supervisors weekly or more often, and two-thirds said they always or often give more to their school community than they get back. Among those who always experienced that imbalance, 57% reported feeling burned out always or very often. Overall, 1 in 4 educators said they were likely to leave their job within a year. Related Taking School Climate and Student Belonging One Step Further With ‘Mattering’ Gallup researchers interpreted these sobering findings through a framework of mattering that I developed, called SAID. It consists of four components: significance (do people know me as a person?); appreciation (do people notice and value my contributions?); invested in (is someone supporting my growth and well-being?); and depended on (do others rely on me in sustainable ways?). Feeling appreciation had the strongest link to educators’ sense of mattering, with recognition from supervisors outweighing that of students or parents. Among the four SAID dimensions, feeling invested had the strongest relationship with educators’ likelihood of quitting within the next year. Teachers know they are needed. But that is only part of what it means to matter. This echoes what researchers call the passion tax — the expectation that people will accept extra work, low pay or little support because they love what they do. Devotion to your students shouldn’t mean ignoring your own needs and limits. This isn’t just an issue for schools: Parents have a stake in the mattering crisis, too. As is commonly noted, educators’ working conditions become students’ learning conditions . In other words, caring for teachers is also a way to care for children. Mattering is not a slogan. It’s built from the accumulation of everyday signals educators receive from colleagues, supervisors, students and parents, and it erodes when those signals go missing. The survey findings offer a lens and a shared language for understanding where educators’ experiences are falling short and where schools might focus their attention. Here are some steps schools and parents can take to bridge the mattering gap: Schools can make appreciation a regular part of staff meetings and supervisor check-ins by recognizing both the contribution and the person, by saying, for example: “You have a gift for helping students see their own potential.” Schools can also invest in educators’ growth by asking what they need to succeed and then following through. This can include providing dedicated time for mentoring and collaboration, offering professional development teachers actually want and giving them a voice in decisions that affect their classrooms. Parents can ask themselves: How often do teachers hear from us when something goes wrong, compared with when we appreciate something they’ve done? Even a short, positive message — “Because of your enthusiasm and patience, my son loves math again” — can connect educators to their impact. These practices belong alongside adequate pay, full staffing and manageable workloads as choices that communicate just how much educators matter. The mattering gap is a wake-up call. School and parents can start addressing it today. Just as families and communities depend on educators to help children thrive, all of us need to make sure those educators feel valued and supported so they will, too.
